Badejo As Mia Mottley rightly said, the issue is not only who sits at the table but how power is exercised. When, and if, the seat comes, that will be the test. by Premium Times October 19, 2026 Reading Time: 8 mins read 0 Add us on Google Africa should keep pushing for the restructuring of the Security Council, even if it will not be realised soon. But African unity would be severely tested if the continent were asked today to name the countries that would occupy the two permanent seats, without veto, which the Biden administration said in September 2024 it would support. Washington knows how hard it is for any region to agree on the occupants of new seats.
The 81st UN General Assembly met under the theme “Restoring trust, managing transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all.” I followed the General Debate closely. For different reasons, leader after leader called for reform of the United Nations. Small countries want the Security Council restructured, above all to broaden its representation. Some also want an end to the veto wielded by its five permanent members: China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States.
As I listened, I kept wondering whether Africa will ever have a permanent place at the table where war and peace are decided, and on what grounds it should continue to press for one.
By a tradition dating back to 1955, Brazil opened the General Debate on 22 September. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defended multilateralism at a time when the major powers increasingly prefer unilateralism. He renewed Brazil’s long-standing call to enlarge the Security Council with new permanent members.
President Donald Trump followed, as the host country’s leader traditionally does. Defending the war against Iran, he told the Assembly that “while others have talked, I have acted,” and said he had to decide between a deal with Tehran and annihilating it. He called the International Criminal Court “an evil group of people” and urged its member states to leave it. Africa hardly featured; the deals with Africa were struck on the sidelines.
Prime Minister Mia Amor Mottley of Barbados, a source of pride to Africans on the continent and in the diaspora, continues to make strides far beyond Barbados. In a world in which African voices are becoming endangered, I admire her boldness on many issues. Of course, that same boldness rules her out of the pool of women being considered to succeed António Guterres.

In her address to the Assembly on 24 September, she called for the Caribbean to remain a zone of peace. On Haiti, she backed the full, long-promised deployment of the 5,500-strong Gang Suppression Force and the renewal of its mandate, and she did not mince words: “Enough is enough.” She spoke up for Cuba and for dialogue grounded in sovereign equality.
She linked slavery to today’s global order. She argued that the mindset that built and sustained slavery is the same one that preserves inequities in the UN’s own power structures and in the international financial architecture. She also insisted that the Caribbean does not ask for reparations without accepting responsibility for its own self-repair. No African leader said it better. In that hall, Mottley was an African speaking for all Africans.
She also put the reform question more sharply than anyone. While supporting permanent membership of the Security Council for Africa, and probably for the Caribbean, she rightly pointed out that the issue is not only who sits at the table, but how power at that table is exercised. Africa should keep that sentence in its pocket.
President John Dramani Mahama of Ghana spoke in the tradition of Nkrumah. He noted that Africa, with 1.5 billion people, is home to over 18 per cent of humanity and forms the largest regional voting bloc in the General Assembly. On that basis, he demanded permanent African representation on the Security Council with full veto powers.
He highlighted the March 2026 resolution, tabled by Ghana and backed by 123 nations, declaring the transatlantic slave trade the gravest crime against humanity; the same resolution Mia Mottley celebrated. He argued that true repair means dismantling unfair trade regimes, discriminatory credit ratings, unsustainable debt and the export of raw materials without value addition. He insisted that Africa’s critical minerals be processed on the continent. Twice, he condemned corruption in Africa.
Africa should argue from development. It has 1.5 billion people, the world’s youngest population, the minerals on which the energy transition depends, a continental free trade area, and a legitimate grievance that the rules of finance, trade and climate are written without it. That was Mahama at his best, and Ruto on credit ratings. A continent that asks for power in order to lift its people out of poverty makes a stronger case than one that asks for power because it keeps appearing on the Council’s crisis list.
President William Ruto of Kenya pointed out that every nation has one vote in the Assembly, yet on war and peace five nations hold a permanent power that the other 188 do not. Africa, with 54 member states and more than a quarter of the Assembly, has no permanent voice and is too often the subject of Council decisions: “permanently discussed, yet permanently excluded.” He answered the claim that reform is impossible by recalling that in 1963 the Assembly amended the Charter to enlarge the Council from eleven to fifteen members.
He noted that developing countries borrow at rates two to four times higher than developed nations, and that biased credit ratings have cost Africa about $75 billion. To his credit, he conceded that reform abroad cannot substitute for accountability at home, including confronting corruption without equivocation.
Nigeria spoke through Vice President Kashim Shettima, who delivered President Bola Tinubu’s statement. He demanded at least two permanent seats for Africa, with the veto for as long as it exists, and five non-permanent seats, in line with the Ezulwini Consensus and the Sirte Declaration. His best line was that “the world of 2026 cannot remain captive to the distribution of power in 1945.” He said Nigeria is ready for greater responsibility, citing its sacrifices in Liberia, Sierra Leone, Mali and The Gambia, and its mediation and security work through ECOWAS, the AU and in the Gulf of Guinea.
Having served in several of those theatres, I can confirm that Nigeria’s peacekeeping record is real. But, as the lawyers say, past consideration is no consideration. Nigeria’s sacrifices in Liberia, Sierra Leone and elsewhere are honourable, but they now belong to the archives. A permanent seat is not a reward for what a country did in the 1990s; it is a bet on what it can deliver today. And a Nigeria that cannot secure its own highways will struggle to persuade the world that it can carry the weight of a permanent seat with a veto.
Here I part company with an argument I heard too often that week. It runs like this: because the Council spends so much of its time on Sudan, Somalia, South Sudan, the Sahel and eastern Congo, Africa deserves a permanent seat to shape those decisions. Ruto’s phrase “permanently discussed” captures a real frustration. But I do not accept that a continent’s conflicts are its qualifications.
Conflict is a symptom of failures of governance and development, many of them home-made. A claim built on being the Council’s most frequent agenda item is a claim built on a negative attribute. Peacekeeping sacrifices, real as Nigeria’s have been, prove commitment. They do not prove the capacity to prevent the next war.
Africa should argue from development. It has 1.5 billion people, the world’s youngest population, the minerals on which the energy transition depends, a continental free trade area, and a legitimate grievance that the rules of finance, trade and climate are written without it. That was Mahama at his best, and Ruto on credit ratings. A continent that asks for power in order to lift its people out of poverty makes a stronger case than one that asks for power because it keeps appearing on the Council’s crisis list.
I agree with Mia Amor Mottley, a great daughter of Africa rising in the mould of Mandela and Nkrumah: the issue is not only the seat, but how power is exercised from it. We have run this experiment before. When Jeffrey Sachs argued that Africa should be given a seat at the G20, I argued against treating the seat itself as the solution. My point was that a seat feeds no hungry child; what matters is how Africa’s leaders use it, and whether governance improves at home.
Africa got the seat. The AU formally joined the G20 in New Delhi on 9 September, 2023. It attended its first summit as a full member in Rio de Janeiro in November 2024, and in November 2025 the G20 met on African soil for the first time, in Johannesburg.
What has changed for Africa’s poor? According to the World Bank’s April 2025 Africa’s Pulse , about 80 per cent of the world’s estimated 695 million extremely poor people lived in Sub-Saharan Africa in 2024. The Bank projected that the region’s number of extremely poor people would rise by 90 million between 2022 and 2027. Nigeria alone accounts for 19 per cent of the region’s extreme poor, over 106 million people.
A seat at the G20 has not moved those numbers. Without improved capacity at home, a seat becomes a photo opportunity with a flag.
As Mia Mottley rightly said, the issue is not only who sits at the table but how power is exercised. When, and if, the seat comes, that will be the test. With 54 of the 193 members of the General Assembly, Africa has no excuse for failing to produce a clear leader: a country able to pay its own bills and lift its people out of squalor and poverty.
Still, I must be realistic about the permanent seat. Any enlargement requires a Charter amendment. It needs a two-thirds vote in the General Assembly and then ratification by two-thirds of member states, including all five permanent members, any one of whom can block it.
The hurdles are real. There is the veto question. There is the Uniting for Consensus bloc. And there is Africa’s own unresolved question of which two countries would sit: Nigeria, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia and Kenya are all in contention, while smaller countries pushed at Ezulwini for any seat granted to Africa to rotate. Together, these make Africa’s desire look like a mirage.
Yet there are openings. The Pact for the Future commits member states to redress the historical injustice against Africa as a priority, and 1963 shows that the Charter can move. A new Secretary-General takes office in January 2027, and Ghana is due to chair the AU that year. Africa must settle on its candidates, speak with one voice, and argue from development rather than distress. Then the seat is no longer a dream deferred; it becomes a negotiation the P5 cannot postpone indefinitely.
HE Abdoulkader Houssein Omar, Djibouti’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, delivered his country’s statement on 26 September. He drew attention to the thousands of people fleeing Yemen into Djibouti’s Obock region. He urged the world to preserve the security gains in Somalia. He welcomed Sudan’s return to IGAD, which Djibouti currently chairs, and called for curbs on negative external interference in Sudan.
He reminded the Assembly of the Djiboutian prisoners of war held incommunicado by Eritrea for more than eighteen years. Like many African states, and indeed much of the world, Djibouti expressed solidarity with the Palestinian people and support for the two-state solution.
The Minister also devoted time to development, under the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals and the AU’s Agenda 2063. He informed the Assembly that Djibouti is building a national carbon-market framework under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. He demanded that the Seville Commitment on financing for development deliver concessional finance and debt sustainability. Djibouti’s voice carries beyond its size.
Africa should keep pushing for the restructuring of the Security Council, even if it will not be realised soon. But African unity would be severely tested if the continent were asked today to name the countries that would occupy the two permanent seats, without veto, which the Biden administration said in September 2024 it would support. Washington knows how hard it is for any region to agree on the occupants of new seats.
So why damage relations over something that is not about to happen, given the known differences on this issue within Africa, Europe, South and South-East Asia, and Latin America? Africa needs to argue from strength, focusing on its development challenges, including the more consequential vetoes at the Bretton Woods institutions.
As Mia Mottley rightly said, the issue is not only who sits at the table but how power is exercised. When, and if, the seat comes, that will be the test. With 54 of the 193 members of the General Assembly, Africa has no excuse for failing to produce a clear leader: a country able to pay its own bills and lift its people out of squalor and poverty.
Babafemi A. Badejo is a former Deputy Special Representative of the UN Secretary-General for Somalia and a former Professor of Political Science and International Relations. He is the author of the best-selling Raila Odinga: An Enigma in Kenyan Politics and of Somalia Just Before Al-Shabaab: Why Peace Was Elusive. He is a recipient of the Mandela Lifetime Achievement Award of the Annual Africa Conference at the University of Texas at Austin, the Medal of the Order of Timor-Leste, and Djibouti’s 27 Juin 1977 Order.
